title: XOR circuits for the quadratic-residue circulant
statement: For a prime p let Q_p be the p x p circulant matrix over GF(2) with Q[i][j] = 1 exactly when j - i is a nonzero square modulo p (its rows span the quadratic-residue codes of length p). An XOR circuit (linear straight-line program) for Q_p starts from the inputs x_0, ..., x_(p-1), adds gates s = a XOR b of earlier signals, and must produce every output y_i = sum over j of Q[i][j] x_j as one of its signals. What is the smallest number of gates? The headline cell is p = 31: find a circuit with fewer than 238 gates.
submission: Text file: a first line '31 G', then G lines 'a b' (gate k is signal 30 + k, the XOR of signals a and b, which must be inputs 0..30 or earlier gates), then one line of 31 signal numbers giving outputs y_0, ..., y_30 in order.
score: G, the number of XOR gates (smaller is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: Paar's greedy common-pair elimination, best of 60 randomized runs (tools/qr_xor.py)

context: The smallest XOR circuit for a fixed GF(2)-linear map is the shortest linear program problem, NP-hard in general and attacked with heuristics and SAT solvers (Boyar, Matthews and Peralta, J. Cryptology 26 (2013)); it is studied intensively for the diffusion matrices of block ciphers, where every saved gate makes a smaller implementation (Kranz, Leander, Stoffelen and Wiemer, ToSC 2017). The quadratic-residue circulants encode the classical quadratic-residue codes (MacWilliams and Sloane, chapter 16) and have a large symmetry group (x -> ax + b with a a nonzero square), so they test whether symmetry can be turned into sharing: for p = 7 the residues {1, 2, 4} form a perfect difference set, every pair of inputs lies in exactly one row, and no cancellation-free sharing is possible (14 gates); for p = 31 the greedy method already saves 45 percent (238 gates against 434).
references: C. Paar, Optimized arithmetic for Reed-Solomon encoders, IEEE ISIT 1997 (the greedy common-pair method)
J. Boyar, P. Matthews, R. Peralta, Logic minimization techniques with applications to cryptology, J. Cryptology 26 (2013) 280-312
T. Kranz, G. Leander, K. Stoffelen, F. Wiemer, Shorter linear straight-line programs for MDS matrices, IACR Trans. Symmetric Cryptology 2017(4) 188-211
F. J. MacWilliams, N. J. A. Sloane, The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes (North-Holland, 1977), chapter 16 (quadratic-residue codes)

novelty.verdict: new. No XOR count or straight-line program for quadratic-residue circulants was found on arXiv or by web search; published XOR-count work concerns MDS diffusion matrices and general heuristics.
closest: Straight-line programs for MDS diffusion matrices and block circulant MDS matrices (Kranz et al. 2017 and later work): the same question for different matrices.

first_values.note: Upper bounds from 60 randomized runs of Paar's greedy method (cancellation-free). Circuits that use cancellation (as in the Boyar-Peralta heuristic) may do better; no lower bound beyond the trivial p is proved.

baseline.text: 238 gates for p = 31, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the circuit in `refs/qr-xor.txt` (Paar's greedy method, tools/qr_xor.py). Lower bound: 31 (the 31 outputs are distinct and none is an input, so each is a different gate); nothing better is proved.

bound.source: the 31 outputs are distinct non-input signals
